cards.title: Introduction to Background Tasks
cards.content:
In standard web applications, the request-response cycle must be fast. If a user triggers an action that takes a long time—like sending an email, processing an image, or generating a heavy PDF—the HTTP request will hang, leading to a poor user experience.

Background tasks allow offloading these heavy operations to worker processes that run asynchronously outside the main request thread.

options.text: To make the HTTP request block until the heavy task finishes.
To prevent HTTP requests from timing out during long-running operations.
To replace the database entirely with a message queue.
To serve static HTML files faster.

cards.title: Celery and Message Brokers
cards.content:
Celery is the most popular task queue implementation for Python and Flask. To use Celery, you need a message broker that transmits messages between your Flask app and the Celery workers.

Common brokers include:

  • Redis (Fast, in-memory, very popular)
  • RabbitMQ (Robust, feature-rich AMQP broker)
from celery import Celery

def make_celery(app):
    celery = Celery(
        app.import_name,
        backend=app.config['CELERY_RESULT_BACKEND'],
        broker=app.config['CELERY_BROKER_URL']
    )
    class ContextTask(celery.Task):
        def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
            with app.app_context():
                return self.run(*args, **kwargs)
    celery.Task = ContextTask
    return celery

content.text: To set up Celery in Flask, we typically use {blank_1} or RabbitMQ as the message broker.

cards.title: Defining and Calling Celery Tasks
cards.content:
Once Celery is initialized, you define tasks using the @celery.task decorator. Instead of calling the function directly, you use the .delay() method to trigger it asynchronously.

@celery.task
def send_async_email(email_address):
    # Simulate sending email
    time.sleep(5)
    print(f"Email sent to {email_address}")

@app.route('/register', methods=['POST'])
def register():
    # Register user logic...
    user_email = request.form['email']
    
    # Trigger background task
    send_async_email.delay(user_email)
    
    return "Registration successful! Check your email soon.", 202

content.instructions: Place the lifecycle steps of a Flask background task in the correct chronological order.

items.text: Client makes an HTTP POST request to a Flask route.
Flask route calls task.delay() to enqueue the job.
Message broker (Redis) receives and holds the task message.
Celery worker pulls the task from the broker and executes it.

cards.title: Lighter Alternatives: Flask-Executor
cards.content:
If your application doesn't need a heavy distributed task queue like Celery, setting up Redis and worker processes might be overkill.

For simpler needs, libraries like Flask-Executor allow you to run tasks concurrently using standard threads or processes within the same application instance.

from flask_executor import Executor

executor = Executor(app)

@app.route('/process')
def process():
    executor.submit(heavy_task, arg1, arg2)
    return "Task submitted!"

options.text: Always use Celery, even for simple single-server apps.
Choose Celery for distributed, heavy, or scalable background workloads, and simpler thread pools (like Flask-Executor) for lightweight local tasks.
Never run background tasks in Flask; always do synchronous processing.
Background tasks cannot access database models.
